note: Attacker-controlled pcap file bytes are written to disk for offline processing.
The pcap file is opened; the global header specifies linktype 220 (DLT_USB_LINUX_MMAPPED) and snaplen 1, causing a 1-byte buffer allocation.

code: p->bufsize = p->snapshot; if (p->bufsize > 2048) p->bufsize = 2048; p->buffer = malloc(p->bufsize)
note: With snaplen=1, the packet buffer is allocated as 1 byte, so any read beyond offset 0 is out-of-bounds.
The packet header declares caplen=1, so only 1 byte of packet data is read into the 1-byte buffer.
fixup_pcap_pkthdr is called with data pointing to the 1-byte buffer; no caplen check is performed before accessing USB header fields.
The 1-byte buffer is cast to pcap_usb_header_mmapped (64 bytes), creating an undersized pointer for subsequent field accesses.
Reads usb_hdr->data_flag at offset 15, which is 14 bytes beyond the 1-byte allocated buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read.
Reads usb_hdr->ndesc at offset 60 and usb_hdr->urb_len at offset 40, both far beyond the 1-byte buffer, triggering the memory-safety violation.
